verses.text: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, unto the church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints which are in all Achaia:
Grace be to you and peace from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ.
Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort;
Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.
For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ.

And whether we be afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation, which is effectual in the enduring of the same sufferings which we also suffer: or whether we be comforted, it is for your consolation and salvation.
And our hope of you is stedfast, knowing, that as ye are partakers of the sufferings, so shall ye be also of the consolation.
For we would not, brethren, have you ignorant of our trouble which came to us in Asia, that we were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life:
But we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead:
Who delivered us from so great a death, and doth deliver: in whom we trust that he will yet deliver us;
Ye also helping together by prayer for us, that for the gift bestowed upon us by the means of many persons thanks may be given by many on our behalf.

For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward.
For we write none other things unto you, than what ye read or acknowledge; and I trust ye shall acknowledge even to the end;
As also ye have acknowledged us in part, that we are your rejoicing, even as ye also are ours in the day of the Lord Jesus.
And in this confidence I was minded to come unto you before, that ye might have a second benefit;
And to pass by you into Macedonia, and to come again out of Macedonia unto you, and of you to be brought on my way toward Judaea.
When I therefore was thus minded, did I use lightness? or the things that I purpose, do I purpose according to the flesh, that with me there should be yea yea, and nay nay?
But as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay.
For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, even by me and Silvanus and Timotheus, was not yea and nay, but in him was yea.
For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us.
Now he which stablisheth us with you in Christ, and hath anointed us, is God;
Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts.
Moreover I call God for a record upon my soul, that to spare you I came not as yet unto Corinth.
Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand.

chapters.summary: Paul writes as "an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, unto the church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints which are in all Achaia," and then does something he does not do in the first letter: instead of thanking God for his readers he blesses God outright — "Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort." The word comfort then dominates the paragraph, and it moves in a circuit rather than a straight line, since God "comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God." Affliction and consolation are yoked in fixed proportion — "as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ" — and both are turned outward toward the congregation, so that "whether we be afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation, which is effectual in the enduring of the same sufferings which we also suffer: or whether we be comforted, it is for your consolation and salvation." On that basis he can say "our hope of you is stedfast, knowing, that as ye are partakers of the sufferings, so shall ye be also of the consolation." Only then does he name the concrete crisis he has been generalizing from: "our trouble which came to us in Asia, that we were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life." He does not soften the account, and he assigns it a purpose — "we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead" — before laying out deliverance in three tenses, past, present, and future: "Who delivered us from so great a death, and doth deliver: in whom we trust that he will yet deliver us." The Corinthians are given a share in that outcome, "Ye also helping together by prayer for us, that for the gift bestowed upon us by the means of many persons thanks may be given by many on our behalf." From here the letter turns defensive. Paul's boast is not achievement but integrity: "our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward," and his letters carry no hidden layer, "for we write none other things unto you, than what ye read or acknowledge." He recalls the itinerary he had promised — "I was minded to come unto you before, that ye might have a second benefit; And to pass by you into Macedonia, and to come again out of Macedonia unto you" — and confronts the accusation the change produced: "did I use lightness? or the things that I purpose, do I purpose according to the flesh, that with me there should be yea yea, and nay nay?" The answer escalates a complaint about travel plans into christology. "But as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, even by me and Silvanus and Timotheus, was not yea and nay, but in him was yea. For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us." The guarantee behind both the message and the messengers is God's own action in four verbs: "he which stablisheth us with you in Christ, and hath anointed us, is God; Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts." Paul closes the chapter under oath, giving the real reason for the delay — "I call God for a record upon my soul, that to spare you I came not as yet unto Corinth" — and immediately disowns the very leverage he has just exercised: "Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand."
takeaways: The opening is a blessing rather than a thanksgiving, and the difference matters. Where the first letter begins "I thank my God always on your behalf," this one begins "Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort" — praise directed at God's character rather than at anything currently visible in the Corinthians. After a painful visit, a severe letter, and a congregation that has been questioning his motives, Paul has less to say about them and everything to say about the God who is "the Father of mercies." A relationship under strain is not repaired here by flattery or by a truce; it is reopened by naming what God is, so that whatever is said afterward about grievances stands inside that frame.

Comfort in this chapter is not a private consolation but a transferable good, and the sentence that says so is deliberately circular: God "comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God." The purpose clause is the point. What is received is not stored, and the qualification to console is not natural sympathy or good technique but having actually been consoled by God in one's own tribulation. This makes affliction the training ground of usefulness rather than an interruption of it, and it means the comfort a sufferer receives already belongs, in part, to someone he has not yet met.

The proportion Paul states is exact and unsentimental: "as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ." Consolation does not arrive as the cancellation of suffering but as its companion, scaled to it, and both come through the same person. He then refuses to let either half be private property — "whether we be afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation... or whether we be comforted, it is for your consolation and salvation" — so that every state he can possibly be in is already ordered toward the church. The logic also runs forward: "as ye are partakers of the sufferings, so shall ye be also of the consolation," which makes shared suffering the ground of a confident hope about people who have been treating him badly.

Paul's report of the crisis in Asia is remarkable for how little he protects his own reputation. He was "pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life," and "we had the sentence of death in ourselves" — no claim to serene faith under pressure, and no suggestion that despair was a failure to be hidden. The purpose clause reframes it without denying it: the sentence of death came "that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead." Resurrection is invoked not as a doctrine about the last day but as the only adequate object of trust for a man who has run out of resources, and the deliverance is then held in three tenses at once — "Who delivered us from so great a death, and doth deliver: in whom we trust that he will yet deliver us" — so that a single past rescue becomes the pattern for the present and the pledge for the future.

The apostle who has just described himself as the church's comforter immediately makes himself the church's debtor: "Ye also helping together by prayer for us, that for the gift bestowed upon us by the means of many persons thanks may be given by many on our behalf." His deliverance is described as coming "by the means of many persons," which credits the prayers of a congregation that had been quarrelling with him, and the intended result is not merely his survival but a widened chorus of thanksgiving. The traffic in this chapter runs both directions, and the same instinct surfaces again in the four verbs of the closing paragraph, where Paul cannot even describe his own standing without including them: it is God "which stablisheth us with you in Christ."

A dispute about a changed itinerary is answered with the character of God rather than with an alibi. Accused of "lightness" and of purposing "according to the flesh," Paul does not chiefly argue that his reasons were good; he argues that his message admits no double-mindedness, since "the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us... was not yea and nay, but in him was yea. For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen." The claim is that a preacher whose subject is God's unqualified Yes cannot conduct his affairs as a series of qualified maybes — his reliability is derivative, borrowed from the content he carries. The mention of the Amen also gathers up the congregation's own liturgical response, so that the church's assent in worship is itself evidence of the argument.

The last two verses hold an unusual tension. Paul swears an oath — "I call God for a record upon my soul" — and uses it to reveal that his absence was mercy: "to spare you I came not as yet unto Corinth." The silence they read as unreliability was restraint, which means he has been exercising authority precisely by not showing up. And in the same breath he disowns the category: "Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand." The disclaimer arrives at the exact moment his power is most evident, and it names both the limit and the aim of pastoral office — faith is not something a minister can command, joy is what he exists to serve, and the church's standing rests on faith rather than on him.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 40:1 — Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God
crossRefs.why: Paul's title for God, "the God of all comfort," is not a general pleasantry but draws on the prophetic vocabulary in which comfort is what God speaks to a people after judgment and exile. Isaiah's comfort is addressed to those whose "warfare is accomplished" and is delivered through human messengers commanded to speak it, which is exactly the circuit Paul describes when consolation received from God is passed on to "them which are in any trouble." Reading the source shows that comfort in Scripture is an event of God's speech and rescue, not a mood.

crossRefs.label: Job 16:2 — miserable comforters are ye all
crossRefs.why: Job's friends are the counter-example that clarifies Paul's rule. They arrive with explanations they have never had to live through, and Job names the result exactly. Paul's qualification to console is stated in the opposite terms: he can comfort others only "by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God," and he establishes his credentials by admitting he "despaired even of life." Set against Job's speech, the chapter reads as a description of what comfort must cost the comforter before it is worth anything to the afflicted.

crossRefs.label: Ezekiel 37:3 — Son of man, can these bones live?
crossRefs.why: Paul's phrase for the object of his trust — "God which raiseth the dead" — is a standing Jewish description of God, and Ezekiel supplies its most vivid picture: a valley of bones belonging to a people who say "our hope is lost," restored by the word and the Spirit. The parallel illuminates why Paul reaches for resurrection language to describe surviving a crisis in Asia rather than reserving it for the last day. In both texts the same God is the only available hope precisely at the point where the situation is beyond repair.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 5:37 — let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay
crossRefs.why: Paul's rhetorical question about whether "with me there should be yea yea, and nay nay" trades on the same idiom Jesus uses, and the two passages together frame the chapter's question about sincerity. The Sermon demands speech so plain that oaths become unnecessary; Paul insists his word "was not yea and nay" and then, at the close of the chapter, calls God "for a record upon my soul." Reading them side by side sharpens the question of what Christ actually forbids and what Paul thinks he is free to do.

crossRefs.label: Acts 19 — the whole city was filled with confusion... at Ephesus
crossRefs.why: Luke narrates the sustained danger of Paul's long Ephesian ministry, including the silversmiths' riot, and Ephesus is in the province Paul calls Asia. Whether or not this is the precise episode behind "our trouble which came to us in Asia," the narrative supplies the kind of pressure Paul assumes his readers already know something about, and it shows the same period in which he formed and then altered the travel plans he is defending here.

crossRefs.label: Ephesians 1:13-14 — sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, Which is the earnest of our inheritance
crossRefs.why: The two images Paul uses in one breath here — "sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts" — appear together again with an added phrase that explains the second: the Spirit is the earnest "of our inheritance," a real first installment of something not yet possessed in full. The parallel keeps the verse from being read either as a bare metaphor or as the whole gift already delivered, and it clarifies why Paul can appeal to the Spirit both as present security and as pledge of a future not yet in hand.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 4:7 — we have this treasure in earthen vessels
crossRefs.why: The theology compressed into this chapter's opening is worked out at length three chapters later, where being "troubled on every side, yet not distressed" and "always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus" makes the same claim as "the sufferings of Christ abound in us." The later passage also repeats the outward direction of the suffering — "death worketh in us, but life in you" — and supplies the stated reason for the whole arrangement, "that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us," which is the same purpose given for the sentence of death in Asia.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "whether we be afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation" together with "the sufferings of Christ abound in us" as evidence that the suffering of a member of Christ's body is genuinely fruitful for others. On this account Paul's afflictions are not merely an occasion from which the Corinthians can draw a lesson; they are a real participation in Christ's own passion, joined to it and made useful by it, which is why Paul can say his tribulation is ordered toward their salvation. The same instinct stands behind Paul's willingness elsewhere to speak of "filling up that which is behind of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh for his body's sake." Catholic interpreters are careful to add that nothing is lacking in Christ's atoning work itself; what is being described is the way the members share in what the Head has accomplished, so that offering one's sufferings for others is a real participation and never a supplement.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the phrase in a strictly ministerial and pastoral sense. Paul's afflictions serve the Corinthians because they are the cost of the apostolic mission that brought them the gospel and because his endurance and rescue become the pattern and the proof of the comfort he then hands on — "which is effectual in the enduring of the same sufferings which we also suffer." On this view the benefit is real but instrumental and exemplary rather than expiatory, and the sufferings of Christ that abound in Paul are the sufferings endured for Christ's sake and in union with him, not a share in the work of atonement, which the same letter treats as finished and sufficient. Both traditions agree that Christ's sacrifice is unrepeatable and that Paul's phrase says something more than that his pain merely happened to be educational for onlookers.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "he which stablisheth us with you in Christ, and hath anointed us, is God; Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts," the Catholic tradition hears the vocabulary of sacramental initiation. Anointing and sealing describe what is done to a Christian in baptism and confirmation, an act of God that leaves a permanent mark and configures the person to Christ, and the Spirit given as "the earnest" is real grace truly indwelling and not merely promised. Because the gift is an earnest rather than the inheritance itself, Catholic reading holds together two things: the seal is God's own work and cannot be counterfeited or self-generated, and it is nevertheless a pledge held by someone still on the way, whose final possession of the inheritance depends on remaining in the grace that has been given.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings emphasize the commercial force of the image: an earnest is a down payment that legally guarantees the rest, so the Spirit's presence functions as God's own security for a salvation certain to be completed. Reformed interpreters in particular read the sealing as the ground of assurance and of final perseverance, since the guarantor is God and the four verbs of the sentence all take God as their subject; the believer's confidence therefore does not rest on the strength of his grip. Most Protestant traditions locate the sealing at the point of faith rather than tying it to a distinct rite, and evangelical readings especially resist reading confirmation into the anointing. Lutherans and many Anglicans stand closer to the sacramental reading of baptism while still grounding its power in the promise received by faith. All sides agree the Spirit here is a genuine present possession and not yet the whole inheritance.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic interpretation reads Paul's "I call God for a record upon my soul" as a lawful oath, and takes the chapter as evidence that Christ's saying about "yea, yea" forbids casual, deceptive, or profane swearing rather than every solemn appeal to God. Paul, who elsewhere insists on plain speech, invokes God as witness at a moment of grave necessity when his motives are being publicly impugned and a congregation's trust is at stake, which is precisely the narrow case the tradition allows: an oath sworn in truth, in judgment, and in justice. The reading also keeps Paul's boast in "the testimony of our conscience" from being read as self-righteousness, since he immediately attributes the whole of his conduct not to his own character but to grace — "not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God."

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings divide. The magisterial Reformation traditions agree substantially with the Catholic position, holding that oaths before magistrates and in grave matters are lawful acts of worship and that Paul's practice settles the question. The radical Reformation strand — Anabaptist, and later Quaker — reads Christ's prohibition as absolute and answers that Paul's language is a solemn appeal rather than a formal oath, or that apostolic practice does not license what the Lord plainly forbade; these communities have historically accepted legal penalties rather than swear. All sides agree that the chapter's real concern is Paul's truthfulness, and that his appeal to conscience is offered as evidence rather than as a claim to sinlessness, since he grounds it in grace and not in performance.

interpretationNotes.claim: "Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand" is read in the Catholic tradition as defining the manner of apostolic authority rather than denying its existence. Paul plainly holds authority in this chapter — he changes an announced itinerary, he swears that the change was "to spare you," and the sparing implies that a visit could have been severe. What he disclaims is lordship over the interior act of faith, which cannot be coerced and remains a free response to God. The verse is therefore taken as a description of office exercised for edification: real teaching and governing authority, given for the building up of the faithful and answerable for that purpose, never a proprietary power over another person's soul.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters read the verse as a stronger and more principled limit on ecclesiastical power, and often as a charter against clericalism. They note that Paul settles the dispute by appeal to the gospel he preached and to God's faithfulness rather than by invoking an office, and that "by faith ye stand" locates the believer's standing directly before God, with conscience bound by the word rather than by a human authority. On this reading ministers are servants of the word whose whole warrant is the message they carry, so any claim that outruns Scripture forfeits its ground. Both traditions agree that Paul is exercising genuine pastoral authority at the very moment he disclaims dominion, and that the aim named here — helping the church's joy — is the test by which such authority is judged.

verses.text: But I determined this with myself, that I would not come again to you in heaviness.
For if I make you sorry, who is he then that maketh me glad, but the same which is made sorry by me?
And I wrote this same unto you, lest, when I came, I should have sorrow from them of whom I ought to rejoice; having confidence in you all, that my joy is the joy of you all.
For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote unto you with many tears; not that ye should be grieved, but that ye might know the love which I have more abundantly unto you.
But if any have caused grief, he hath not grieved me, but in part: that I may not overcharge you all.
Sufficient to such a man is this punishment, which was inflicted of many.
So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
Wherefore I beseech you that ye would confirm your love toward him.
For to this end also did I write, that I might know the proof of you, whether ye be obedient in all things.
To whom ye forgive any thing, I forgive also: for if I forgave any thing, to whom I forgave it, for your sakes forgave I it in the person of Christ;
Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices.
Furthermore, when I came to Troas to preach Christ’s gospel, and a door was opened unto me of the Lord,
I had no rest in my spirit, because I found not Titus my brother: but taking my leave of them, I went from thence into Macedonia.
Now thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ, and maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place.
For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish:
To the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life. And who is sufficient for these things?
For we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ.

chapters.summary: The chapter opens with a decision already taken and now explained: "But I determined this with myself, that I would not come again to you in heaviness." Paul had made a painful visit and has chosen not to repeat it, and the reason he gives is not self-protection but a strange kind of mutual dependence — "For if I make you sorry, who is he then that maketh me glad, but the same which is made sorry by me?" The only people who could gladden him are the very people he would have had to wound, so a second grieving visit would have cost him his own joy. He therefore wrote instead of coming: "And I wrote this same unto you, lest, when I came, I should have sorrow from them of whom I ought to rejoice; having confidence in you all, that my joy is the joy of you all." The letter itself he now describes from the inside, and the description is unusually exposed for an apostle defending his authority: "For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote unto you with many tears; not that ye should be grieved, but that ye might know the love which I have more abundantly unto you." Severity is claimed as an act of love, and the tears are offered as evidence. Paul then turns to the man who caused the trouble, and immediately refuses to stand at the centre of the injury: "But if any have caused grief, he hath not grieved me, but in part: that I may not overcharge you all." The offence was against the church, not chiefly against Paul, and Paul will not let the congregation be over-blamed for it either. What follows is the chapter's pastoral hinge. "Sufficient to such a man is this punishment, which was inflicted of many" — the censure the community imposed has done its work and is now to stop. "So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Wherefore I beseech you that ye would confirm your love toward him." Forgiveness here is not a private feeling but a corporate act that must be made visible, and the danger Paul fears is no longer laxity but a repentant man drowned by the discipline meant to save him. He explains why he had pressed so hard: "For to this end also did I write, that I might know the proof of you, whether ye be obedient in all things." Then he binds his own act of pardon to theirs: "To whom ye forgive any thing, I forgive also: for if I forgave any thing, to whom I forgave it, for your sakes forgave I it in the person of Christ;" and he names the stake with a soldier's clarity — "Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices." The narrative then resumes where the letter's opening had left it: "Furthermore, when I came to Troas to preach Christ’s gospel, and a door was opened unto me of the Lord, I had no rest in my spirit, because I found not Titus my brother: but taking my leave of them, I went from thence into Macedonia." An open door is left unentered because a friend is missing and news of Corinth has not come. From that raw admission Paul breaks without transition into one of his great doxologies: "Now thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ, and maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place." The image is a triumphal procession trailing incense, and the incense is read differently by different noses: "For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish: To the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life." The weight of that double effect produces the chapter's last question, "And who is sufficient for these things?", and its immediate answer is negative and moral rather than a boast of competence: "For we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ."
takeaways: Paul grounds his change of travel plans in a piece of pastoral logic that is easy to skip over: "if I make you sorry, who is he then that maketh me glad, but the same which is made sorry by me?" He has no reservoir of joy independent of the people he must correct, and he says so plainly — "my joy is the joy of you all." This makes the chapter's severity structurally different from mere discipline administered from above. A pastor whose gladness is not bound up with his people can wound them at no cost to himself; Paul cannot, and the whole tone of the chapter, including the tears, follows from that.

The severe letter is defended by disclosing the state of the man who wrote it: "out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote unto you with many tears; not that ye should be grieved, but that ye might know the love which I have more abundantly unto you." Paul distinguishes the intended effect of correction from its felt effect. Grief was the unavoidable instrument, not the goal; the goal was that they should know a love they had begun to doubt. The verse quietly rules out two failures at once — correction delivered without anguish, and love that will not risk causing pain.

"But if any have caused grief, he hath not grieved me, but in part" is a deliberate act of self-removal. Paul had every ground to treat the offence as a personal wound, since his authority had been publicly resisted, yet he insists the injury was primarily the community's and adds "that I may not overcharge you all" so that the church is not made to carry more blame than it owes. Two temptations are refused in a single sentence: making oneself the aggrieved party, and letting a whole congregation be indicted for one man's act.

The chapter establishes that church discipline has a terminus built into it. "Sufficient to such a man is this punishment, which was inflicted of many" declares the censure adequate and therefore finished, and "contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him" turns the same authority that imposed it toward release. The stated danger is now the opposite of the original one — "lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow" — and the remedy is not merely lifting a penalty but an active, visible gesture: "confirm your love toward him." A community can sin by refusing to end a punishment as truly as by refusing to begin one.

"Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices" places the whole discipline episode on a battlefield, and reverses the expected direction of the threat. Elsewhere the offender is handed over to Satan; here Satan's opening is the church's own unrelenting rigour, which could destroy through despair the man that discipline was meant to recover. The plural is pointed — the advantage would be gained "of us," over the community, not merely over the sinner. Paul treats unforgiveness as a strategy the enemy is known to use, which is why refusing to forgive is not caution but defeat.

The Troas episode is one of the most humanly transparent moments in Paul's correspondence: "a door was opened unto me of the Lord, I had no rest in my spirit, because I found not Titus my brother: but taking my leave of them, I went from thence into Macedonia." An acknowledged providential opening is left behind because anxiety over a church and a missing colleague made him unable to work. Paul does not present this as failure or as obedience to a special leading; he simply reports it. Placed immediately before "thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ," it defines what the triumph is not — it is not the absence of restlessness, dead ends, or abandoned opportunities.

The savour imagery makes the preacher's effect independent of the preacher's intent. The same aroma rises from the same ministry, yet "To the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life," and both are described as being "unto God a sweet savour of Christ" — the offering is acceptable regardless of how it is received. This is why the question "who is sufficient for these things?" is not rhetorical modesty. Nothing in a minister's competence controls the outcome, so the only thing left within his power is integrity, which is exactly where Paul goes next: not to corrupt the word of God, but to speak "as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God."

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 5 — deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved
crossRefs.why: The earlier letter had commanded a severe excommunication and stated its aim as salvation, not destruction, which is precisely the aim this chapter now says has been reached. Whether the man of 2 Corinthians 2 is the same offender or a later ringleader of the revolt against Paul is disputed, but the two chapters read together supply the full arc that neither shows alone: a censure imposed with a stated redemptive purpose, and then a censure lifted because that purpose is judged accomplished — "Sufficient to such a man is this punishment."

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 7 — godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of
crossRefs.why: Paul breaks off the Troas narrative at verse 13 and resumes it only here, with the meeting he was longing for: "when we were come into Macedonia... God, that comforteth those that are cast down, comforted us by the coming of Titus." The later chapter also completes the theology of the severe letter, distinguishing the sorrow that produces repentance from "the sorrow of the world" that "worketh death" — which is the very sorrow Paul fears will swallow up the forgiven man.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 18 — whatsoever ye shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatsoever ye shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven
crossRefs.why: Jesus lays out the same sequence Paul is working through: escalating correction whose purpose is to "gain thy brother," a communal verdict, an authority to bind and to loose that heaven honours, and then the parable of a servant forgiven a vast debt who refuses a small one. Paul's "To whom ye forgive any thing, I forgive also" assumes exactly this loosing power exercised by the assembly, and the parable's ending explains why refusing to use it would hand Satan an advantage.

crossRefs.label: John 20:23 — Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained
crossRefs.why: The risen Christ breathes on the apostles and gives a commission to remit and to retain, which is the clearest New Testament background to Paul forgiving "in the person of Christ." The passage sharpens the interpretive question this chapter raises — whether such forgiveness is a declaration of what God has already done or an act genuinely effective through the minister — and shows that in both readings the authority is derived, exercised only because it was handed over by Christ himself.

crossRefs.label: Ephesians 4:27, 32 — neither give place to the devil... forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you
crossRefs.why: Paul elsewhere makes the same link this chapter compresses into a single clause: nursed anger is described as ground surrendered to the devil, and forgiveness is commanded on the pattern of God's own forgiveness in Christ. Set beside "Lest Satan should get an advantage of us," the parallel confirms that Paul's concern is not a general anxiety about spiritual attack but a specific conviction that an unforgiving community has already given the enemy his foothold.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 8:21 — And the LORD smelled a sweet savour
crossRefs.why: The phrase Paul applies to the apostolic ministry is drawn from the language of sacrifice, where the ascending smoke of an offering is said to be received with pleasure by God. Reading the original scene shows what "we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ" claims: the preacher is not merely a messenger but an offering, and its acceptability is measured by God's reception of it rather than by the response of those who smell it — which is why the same savour can be sweet to God while being death to some who encounter it.

crossRefs.label: Luke 2:34 — this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel; and for a sign which shall be spoken against
crossRefs.why: Simeon announces at the beginning of the gospel the double outcome Paul reports from the middle of his ministry. One and the same Christ causes falling and rising, and the effect is not an accident of presentation but belongs to what he is. This keeps "the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life" from being read as a comment on preaching technique: the division runs back to the person preached, not to the skill or failure of the preacher.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic interpretation reads "if I forgave any thing, to whom I forgave it, for your sakes forgave I it in the person of Christ" as a genuine exercise of a delegated power to remit sins, not a report of Paul's private sentiments. The phrase is taken to mean that Paul acts in Christ's place and with Christ's authority, so that what he and the community loose is really loosed; this is the same authority Christ gave when he sent the apostles to remit and retain sins, and it stands behind the Church's later sacramental practice of absolution pronounced by a minister acting in the person of Christ. On this reading the sequence of the chapter is itself instructive: an offence, a censure imposed by the community, evidence of repentance, a judgment that the penalty is "sufficient," and then a formal reconciliation that restores the man to communion — a recognisable shape of ecclesial penance rather than an informal reconciliation among friends.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the phrase as "in the presence of Christ" or "before the face of Christ," that is, Paul forgiving as one who stands under Christ's own eye, and they note that the forgiveness in view is the church's restoration of a disciplined member to fellowship rather than the absolution of sins before God. The initiative in the verse is given to the congregation — "To whom ye forgive any thing, I forgive also" — with Paul following their act rather than conferring it, which they take as evidence that the power is corporate and declarative rather than priestly. Guilt before God, on this view, is remitted directly through Christ on repentance and faith, while the minister and the assembly announce and enact that pardon within the visible community. Both traditions agree the authority is entirely derived from Christ, that it is exercised for the offender's restoration, and that it is real rather than merely symbolic.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "Sufficient to such a man is this punishment, which was inflicted of many," Catholic reading understands ecclesiastical censure as medicinal and measurable — a penalty proportioned to the offence, imposed by legitimate authority, capable of being judged adequate and therefore remitted. The verse is read as supporting the conviction that repentance is normally accompanied by something borne, some real satisfaction or amendment, and that the Church may fittingly determine and then relax it. That the punishment could be pronounced sufficient implies it was a definite thing with a measure, not merely an attitude, and the lifting of it is an authoritative act rather than a change of mood in the congregation.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings accept that discipline is corrective and that Paul is ending it, but resist any suggestion that the man's suffering satisfies for his sin. The censure is understood as exclusion from fellowship whose whole purpose is to bring him to repentance, so that once repentance appears the censure has no remaining function — "sufficient" meaning it has fully served its end, not that a required quantity of penalty has been paid. Christ's satisfaction is held to be complete, and nothing the sinner bears adds to it. Many also stress that Paul's language throughout is persuasive rather than juridical — "I beseech you that ye would confirm your love toward him" — which they read as pastoral appeal to a congregation rather than the exercise of a penal jurisdiction. Both traditions agree that discipline aimed at restoration must actually stop when restoration occurs, and that prolonging it is itself an offence.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic interpretation takes "lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow" as naming a real and serious danger to the man's soul, not merely to his emotional health. Excessive sorrow that despairs of mercy is understood as spiritually destructive, and the fact that Paul urges haste implies that a repentant believer can genuinely be lost through despair if the community withholds the comfort it owes him. Read with "Lest Satan should get an advantage of us," the verse is taken as evidence that perseverance is not automatic and that the pastoral care of others contributes truly, if instrumentally, to whether they endure — which is why the command to "confirm your love toward him" carries the weight of an obligation rather than a courtesy.

counterpoint.summary: Reformed interpreters hold that those truly in Christ will be preserved and so read the danger as real but not finally fatal: the sorrow could crush the man's assurance, drive him from the visible church, and hand Satan a genuine tactical victory, without meaning that a believer could be irrevocably lost. Arminian and Wesleyan Protestants read the warning much as Catholics do, allowing that grace can be resisted and faith abandoned under despair. Across these differences Protestant readers agree that God ordinarily preserves his people through means, and that the church's comfort is one of those means, so the urgency of Paul's appeal is not diminished by the doctrine of perseverance. All sides read the verse as a warning against a severity that has forgotten its own purpose.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading of "we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish: To the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life" understands the double outcome as arising from the free reception or refusal of a grace genuinely offered to both. The offering is one, and God's will in making it is one; the difference lies in the response, so that those who perish do so by rejecting what was truly held out to them. The sacrificial vocabulary is also heard as ministerial and priestly — the apostle himself an offering made acceptable in Christ — and the answering question, "And who is sufficient for these things?", is taken to expect the reply that sufficiency comes from God while the minister genuinely cooperates with it, an insufficiency of nature met by grace rather than replaced by it.

counterpoint.summary: Reformed readers hear in the same verses a division that originates in God's purpose rather than in human response, noting that Paul designates the two groups simply as "them that are saved" and "them that perish" without assigning a cause on the human side, and that the preacher is a sweet savour to God in both cases — which they take to mean the ministry accomplishes God's end either way. Lutheran and Arminian Protestants resist that inference, holding that God desires all to be saved and that perishing is self-inflicted resistance to a sincere offer. On the question of sufficiency, Protestant interpreters point ahead in the letter to Paul's own answer, that any sufficiency is of God and not of ourselves, and read verse 17 as locating the minister's whole responsibility in integrity rather than efficacy: not corrupting the word, but speaking "as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God." Both traditions agree that the outcome is not produced by the preacher's power and that the same gospel truly divides those who hear it.

verses.text: Do we begin again to commend ourselves? or need we, as some others, epistles of commendation to you, or letters of commendation from you?
Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men:

Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart.
And such trust have we through Christ to God-ward:
Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God;
Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.

But if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance; which glory was to be done away:
How shall not the ministration of the spirit be rather glorious?
For if the ministration of condemnation be glory, much more doth the ministration of righteousness exceed in glory.
For even that which was made glorious had no glory in this respect, by reason of the glory that excelleth.
For if that which is done away was glorious, much more that which remaineth is glorious.
Seeing then that we have such hope, we use great plainness of speech:
And not as Moses, which put a vail over his face, that the children of Israel could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished:
But their minds were blinded: for until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament; which vail is done away in Christ.
But even unto this day, when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart.
Nevertheless when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away.
Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.
But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.

chapters.summary: Paul resumes a self-defence he finds faintly absurd and says so at once: "Do we begin again to commend ourselves? or need we, as some others, epistles of commendation to you, or letters of commendation from you?" Rivals at Corinth evidently arrived carrying written credentials, and Paul answers by pointing at the congregation itself — "Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men" — then presses the metaphor until it stops being a compliment and becomes a covenant claim: they are "manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart." Every term in that sentence is chosen: Christ is the author and Paul only the one through whom the writing was ministered, the ink is the Spirit of the living God, and the writing surface is the human heart rather than the stone of Sinai, which is the prophetic promise of a law written inwardly and a heart of flesh given in place of a heart of stone. The confidence this yields is immediately stripped of any personal claim: "And such trust have we through Christ to God-ward: Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God; Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life." From that antithesis the chapter becomes a sustained argument from the lesser to the greater, and the lesser is conceded in full: "But if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance; which glory was to be done away: How shall not the ministration of the spirit be rather glorious? For if the ministration of condemnation be glory, much more doth the ministration of righteousness exceed in glory." Paul never says Sinai lacked glory; he says it is outshone — "even that which was made glorious had no glory in this respect, by reason of the glory that excelleth" — and that the contrast is finally one of permanence, "for if that which is done away was glorious, much more that which remaineth is glorious." The comparison then turns pastoral and personal: "Seeing then that we have such hope, we use great plainness of speech: And not as Moses, which put a vail over his face, that the children of Israel could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished." At this point the veil migrates from the face of the mediator to the hearing of his people: "But their minds were blinded: for until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament; which vail is done away in Christ. But even unto this day, when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart." Its removal is not a matter of technique or cleverness but of direction — "Nevertheless when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away. Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty" — and the chapter closes by setting the whole church where only one man had stood on the mountain, and doing to them what merely looking never did to him: "But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord."
takeaways: Paul's refusal of "epistles of commendation" is not a rejection of accountability but a claim about what finally authenticates a ministry. Against rivals who carried paperwork, he offers people: "Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men." The letter has two locations at once — inward, in the affection of the apostle who cannot produce it on demand, and public, legible to anyone who cares to look at the changed lives in Corinth. And crucially the authorship is not his. They are "the epistle of Christ ministered by us," so the minister is the one through whom the writing was delivered, never the one whose name is signed. That is what makes the boast safe: Paul is pointing at handwriting that is demonstrably not his own.

The chapter states confidence and disowns competence in the same breath. "Such trust have we through Christ to God-ward" is followed instantly by "Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves," and the disclaimer is pushed further than expected — not merely to do anything, but to think any thing. What is left is a conferred fitness: "our sufficiency is of God; Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament." New covenant ministry is therefore an office one is made able for, not a capacity one brings; the same God who wrote the letter also equipped the courier, which is why the assurance is total and the self-regard is nil.

"For the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life" is not a verdict against Scripture or against law as such, and Paul immediately proves it by calling the very thing he has just called deadly "glorious." The letter in view is the commandment "written and engraven in stones" — holy, God-given, radiant enough that Israel "could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses." The problem is not the standard but its effect on flesh that cannot meet it: a written requirement can specify righteousness and expose failure, but it has no power to produce what it demands. Hence "the ministration of death" and "the ministration of condemnation" are descriptions of an outcome, not insults to Sinai, and the contrast is between two economies, one that inscribes on stone and one that writes with "the Spirit of the living God" on "fleshy tables of the heart."

The argument is concessive rather than polemical, and its logic runs entirely upward. Three times Paul builds the same ladder — if the ministration of death was glorious, "how shall not the ministration of the spirit be rather glorious"; if condemnation had glory, "much more doth the ministration of righteousness exceed in glory"; if what is done away was glorious, "much more that which remaineth is glorious." He never argues that the old was worthless; he argues that it was real and temporary. Verse ten makes the point with unusual delicacy: "even that which was made glorious had no glory in this respect, by reason of the glory that excelleth." Something can be genuinely luminous and still be unable to be seen once a greater light is in the room, and the decisive difference is finally durability — one glory "was to be done away," the other "remaineth."

The veil moves, and where it lands is the chapter's sharpest observation. Moses covers his own face so that Israel "could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished"; now Paul says the same covering has relocated onto the audience, "for until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament," and more bluntly, "when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart." The difficulty in reading the older Scriptures is therefore not primarily textual obscurity but something over the perceiver, which is why the cure is not scholarship or decoding but a change of orientation: "when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away." Paul's own "great plainness of speech" follows from this — a minister of a covenant with nothing fading to conceal has no motive to veil anything.

The final verse takes the most exclusive scene in Israel's history and hands it to everyone. Moses alone went up, and what he brought back had to be hidden; now "we all, with open face" behold "the glory of the Lord," and the beholding is not merely permitted but effective — "changed into the same image from glory to glory." The verbs matter: Israel "could not stedfastly behold," while the church gazes and is transformed by gazing, and the transformation happens to them rather than being achieved by them, "even as by the Spirit of the Lord." This also defines the liberty of verse seventeen. "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty" is not freedom from obligation but freedom from the veil and from the condemnation of a law that could only accuse — the unhindered access of people who no longer have to look away, and who are being made to resemble what they are finally allowed to see.

The whole chapter quietly answers the question it opened with. Paul was asked, in effect, for his credentials; he ends by describing a ministry whose evidence is a congregation being visibly rewritten by the Spirit and progressively conformed to the image of the Lord. The credential and the theology are the same thing. If the new covenant really writes on hearts rather than stone, then the only proof a minister of it can offer is hearts, and the only proper boast is that the handwriting belongs to someone else.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 34:33-35 — till Moses had done speaking with them, he put a vail on his face
crossRefs.why: This is the scene Paul is expounding, and reading it shows how much he is drawing from and how much he is adding. Exodus reports that Moses' face shone from speaking with God, that Israel was afraid to come near, and that he veiled himself after speaking and unveiled himself before the Lord. Paul takes the same facts and supplies a purpose Exodus does not state — that Israel "could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished" — and then transfers the veil from the mediator's face to the reader's heart. Without the source narrative the chapter's central image is unreadable; with it, the argument about fading glory and unveiled faces becomes an interpretation of a specific mountain and a specific stone.

crossRefs.label: Jeremiah 31:33 — I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts
crossRefs.why: Paul's phrase "able ministers of the new testament" and his contrast between writing "not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart" are drawn straight from this promise of a covenant unlike the one made when God took Israel by the hand out of Egypt. Jeremiah supplies both the vocabulary of a new covenant and the specific innovation Paul is claiming has arrived: a law relocated from an external tablet to the interior of the person. It also explains why Paul can say the older ministry was glorious and still passing — Jeremiah himself announced that it would be replaced.

crossRefs.label: Ezekiel 36:26-27 — I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh
crossRefs.why: Ezekiel joins the two halves of Paul's metaphor that Jeremiah leaves separate: the exchange of a stony heart for a heart of flesh, and the giving of God's Spirit as the power that causes obedience rather than merely commanding it. That is precisely the difference between "the letter killeth" and "the spirit giveth life" — a written requirement versus an indwelling cause. The passage also grounds Paul's insistence that the sufficiency is God's and not the minister's, since Ezekiel states repeatedly that God acts for his own name's sake and not for the people's worthiness.

crossRefs.label: Romans 7:10-12 — the commandment, which was ordained to life, I found to be unto death... the law is holy
crossRefs.why: Romans gives the extended defence of the claim this chapter states in a single line. Paul there insists the law is holy, just, and good, and that death came not from the commandment but from sin taking occasion by it, which is exactly how "the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones" can also be called "glorious." Anyone tempted to read "the letter killeth" as a low view of God's written law is answered directly by the parallel argument, where the same apostle refuses that inference in the strongest terms.

crossRefs.label: Romans 11:25 — blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in
crossRefs.why: This chapter's hardest sentences — "their minds were blinded" and "when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart" — are given their fullest treatment in Romans 11, where Paul denies that God has cast away his people, calls the hardening partial and temporary, and warns Gentile believers against boasting over broken branches. Read together, the veil of 2 Corinthians 3 is not a permanent verdict on Israel but a condition awaiting the turning Paul anticipates in "when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away."

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 4:6 — the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ
crossRefs.why: The following chapter is the same argument continued without a break, and it settles several ambiguities. The veil becomes a hiddenness worked by "the god of this world" on "them that are lost"; the "great plainness of speech" is restated as renouncing "the hidden things of dishonesty" and refusing to handle the word of God deceitfully; and the glory contemplated in a glass is finally located in a face, "the face of Jesus Christ," answering the face of Moses that had to be covered. The pairing shows that the unveiled glory of chapter three is not an abstraction but a person.

crossRefs.label: Romans 8:29 — predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son
crossRefs.why: "Changed into the same image from glory to glory" raises the question of what the finished product is, and Romans 8 names it: conformity to the image of the Son, set within a chain that runs from foreknowledge to glorification. The Spirit's role is identical in both places, working within believers who do not know how to pray as they ought, just as here the change occurs "even as by the Spirit of the Lord" rather than by the beholder's effort. Together they present transformation as a real, progressive, and finally certain work with a specified terminus.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life," the Catholic reading takes the contrast to be between two covenantal economies rather than between Scripture and inspiration, or between rules and sincerity. The letter is the Mosaic law considered as an external written demand unaccompanied by grace; it is genuinely from God and genuinely "glorious," and it kills only because it can specify righteousness without conferring the power to perform it. The Spirit gives life because the new covenant does what Jeremiah and Ezekiel promised, writing on "fleshy tables of the heart" and supplying an interior principle of obedience. Catholic interpretation also has a long habit of hearing in this verse a warning about reading Scripture itself: a merely surface reading that stops at the historical letter and never reaches the reality it signifies leaves the reader with the text and without its life, which is why the tradition holds that the literal sense founds and the deeper senses fulfil the reading of the Old Testament in Christ. On neither construal is the verse a license to set aside what God has commanded.

counterpoint.summary: Classical Protestant readings agree that this is not an attack on Scripture and that the law is holy, but typically frame the antithesis as law and gospel rather than as two eras of salvation history. On that reading the letter kills whenever the commandment is presented to a sinner as the way of standing before God, and the Spirit gives life through the promise received by faith; the same passage of Scripture may function as letter or as spirit depending on how it is preached. Many Protestant interpreters press the point further against the allegorical use of the verse, insisting that "letter" means the law's demand and not the plain grammatical sense of the text, and that treating the literal sense as the deadly one has historically licensed readings the text cannot bear. Reformed writers add that the Spirit does not bypass the written word but works through it. All sides agree that Paul himself calls the stone-written ministry glorious, so no reading may end in contempt for the law or for the Old Testament.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic interpretation reads "the epistle of Christ ministered by us" and "able ministers of the new testament" as a real ministerial office, divinely constituted and divinely enabled, not merely a description of useful activity. Paul's dismissal of "letters of commendation" is read as a rejection of self-promotion and of rival credentials, not as a rejection of authorization as such, since he everywhere assumes a commissioned apostolate and elsewhere commends and installs ministers himself. The stress falls on the word made: God "hath made us able ministers," so the fitness for the office is conferred by God rather than possessed by the man, which is exactly why the office can be real without the officeholder having anything to boast of. On this reading the fruit in Corinth authenticates the ministry precisely because Christ is the author and the apostle is the one through whom the writing was ministered.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings generally place the emphasis differently, taking the passage as evidence that ministry is validated by the Spirit's demonstrable work rather than by institutional accreditation. Paul, facing opponents with impressive documentation, appeals to no office, no succession, and no jurisdiction, but to transformed lives and to the gospel he preached; on this view the argument would be blunted if the decisive credential were an authorization Paul could simply have produced. Evangelical and Reformed interpreters also note that the letter is written by Christ and read by "all men," which locates the verification in the public evidence of changed people rather than in a chain of appointment. Most Protestant traditions still affirm a genuine ordained ministry and orderly calling, and both sides agree the chapter's central claim is that the sufficiency is God's alone.

interpretationNotes.claim: On the veil that "remaineth... untaken away in the reading of the old testament," Catholic interpretation takes the removal to be christological and ecclesial together. The Old Testament is not abolished but unveiled, read rightly only when read as finding its end in Christ, and the Church understands itself as the setting in which that reading is handed on, since it received the Scriptures together with the apostolic preaching that discloses their sense. The blindness Paul describes is treated as a real but not final condition, and "when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away" is read with hope rather than as a closed verdict, in keeping with the conviction that God's covenant with Israel is never revoked. The passage is therefore read as a statement about how Scripture is illuminated in Christ, not as a warrant for contempt toward the Jewish people or for discarding the older covenant's writings.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters agree that the veil is removed in Christ and that the Old Testament is rightly read christologically, but locate the unveiling in the Spirit's illumination of the reader rather than in an authoritative interpretive community. Appeal is made to the very structure of Paul's sentence — the turning is to the Lord, and "the Lord is that Spirit" — so that what lifts the veil is conversion and the Spirit's work, which is also the basis for holding that Scripture's saving sense is accessible to ordinary believers. Some Protestant readings press "that which is done away" and "that which remaineth" toward a sharper discontinuity, treating the Mosaic administration as genuinely obsolete rather than fulfilled and retained, while others hold a strongly covenantal continuity closer to the Catholic account. Both traditions reject reading the veil as a permanent divine rejection of Israel, and both take verse sixteen as pointing to a turning still hoped for.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory" as a description of real transformation of the person by grace, not merely of a changed status or a changed self-understanding. The believer is genuinely made different, progressively and by degrees — "from glory to glory" — and the change is worked by the Spirit while being received and cooperated with rather than passively endured. This is one of the texts on which the tradition builds its account of sanctification as an actual participation in divine life, in which grace elevates and renews the person's own faculties, and it connects directly to the chapter's earlier claim that the new covenant writes on hearts rather than stone. The liberty of verse seventeen is understood in the same key: freedom from the veil and from the law's condemnation, given so that a person may finally do what the commandment always asked.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings likewise affirm a real and progressive transformation here, and this verse is among the most commonly cited Protestant texts on sanctification, but they generally insist that this change is not the ground of acceptance before God, which rests on Christ's righteousness received by faith. The emphasis falls on the passive construction — believers "are changed," the agency being "the Spirit of the Lord" — and on the means, since the beholding happens "as in a glass," which many take to be the gospel itself, making the word the instrument of transformation. Reformed interpreters often stress that no cooperation contributes to the change even while insisting the transformed life is necessarily produced; Wesleyan and Holiness traditions read the same verse toward a more thoroughgoing renewal in this life. On "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty," Protestant readings characteristically extend the freedom to include liberty of conscience from requirements not commanded in Scripture. Both traditions agree that the change is the Spirit's work, that it is progressive, and that its terminus is conformity to Christ.
